1:
Charles Ellicott makes the prophet the psalmist of a new Exodus, the hymn built on the older song though with less local colouring, and finds in its opening that confession must be blended with thanksgiving, since only those who have first felt God’s wrath can rightly estimate the comfort he gives. John Gill reaches the same comparison by another road, since the song answers to what Israel sang at the Red sea, that deliverance being typical of salvation by Christ; the day meant is the Gospel day. John Wesley dates it by the event, the recovery of Israel and the conversion of the Gentiles.

Adam Clarke thinks the hymn much better calculated for the Christian church than for the Jewish, and observes that the Jews themselves seem to have applied it to the times of the Messiah. His evidence is a ceremony: on the last day of the feast of tabernacles they fetched water in a golden pitcher from the fountain of Shiloah, carried it through the water-gate into the temple and poured it with wine on the sacrifice as it lay on the altar; the custom is nowhere ordained in the law of Moses, so Clarke takes it for an emblem of future blessings alluding to the third verse. He supports it from the Talmud, which asks why the place was called the house of drawing and answers that from thence they drew the Holy Spirit; and the Targum, he notes, has receiving with joy a new doctrine from the chosen among the righteous, which he takes for the Gospel, asking whether the paraphrast did not speak as a prophet.

Matthew Henry works on the two words thou shalt say. They mean first that the church will have cause to say it, the promise being sure and its blessings rich enough to furnish abundant matter for thanksgiving; and second that she will have a heart to say it, since God crowns his other gifts with the grace to ascribe their glory to him. He also turns the verse against envy: when many are brought home to Christ the right response is not to grudge the reception they find, as the Jews grudged the favour shown to the Gentiles, but to praise God for grace given to others. And he presses the concession hardest of all: even God’s frowns must not put us out of tune for praising him, since he has often just cause to be angry with us while we have never any reason to be angry with him.

John Calvin reads the song as an exhortation with a second purpose, that the promise may be more fully believed, since a form of thanksgiving is put into their mouth and would not have been given if the grounds were not solid. God’s aim in doing good to his church is that the remembrance of his name be extolled, not because he needs praise but because it profits us. He notices too that the whole people is addressed as one man, because it was their duty to be so united, and draws the same requirement for those who wish their prayers accepted. The leading thought he finds is that God, though justly offended, was satisfied with a moderate chastisement and showed himself willing to be pacified.

The particle is contested. Calvin reports that some render it because, but holds it can also mean although, and cites a scholar who finds the Hebrew construction exactly that of a sentence in one of the epistles; Clarke makes the same identification and complains that the Septuagint and Vulgate kept too close to the Hebrew idiom. Whichever rendering is taken, Calvin says, the sentiment matters, since a conviction of God’s anger prompts despair as soon as it seizes the mind and will overwhelm a man unless seasonably counteracted, Satan using every expedient to drive him there.
2:
Charles Ellicott allows the opening to be rendered either God is my salvation or the God of my salvation, and insists that either way salvation means more than deliverance from danger. He marks two features: the rare doubling of the divine name, found in only one other place, and the fact that apart from it the second clause reproduces the older song word for word. Adam Clarke suspects the shorter name is a copyist’s error, arising because a scribe who found a line too short would fill it with as many letters as it would hold and begin the next line with the whole word; he supports the suspicion from manuscripts and four old versions that omit the shorter name, and reports copies that omit the longer or run the two together.

John Gill reads the opening word as doing four things at once: asserting the fact, expressing wonder, excluding every other saviour, and pointing others to the only one worth looking to. John Calvin makes the same word the hinge, but as evidence of a change in the kind of knowledge involved. It is right to behold God’s salvation by faith in the midst of afflictions, but here the prophet speaks of knowledge derived from experience, since a countenance hidden for a time now shines out so that it may be pointed at with the finger. Because punishments fill us with dread and our minds are overclouded by our sins, he describes the change of feeling that comes when God is reconciled; and the prediction relates chiefly to the coming of Christ, which first exhibited it fully. From this he draws an order: confidence proceeds from faith as an effect from its cause, and where faith is wanting there can be no peace of conscience. John Wesley puts it in a line: the salvation was brought to pass not by man but by the almighty power of God.

The drawing of water is promise and duty at once. Keil and Delitzsch hear a prophetic promise pointing back to the opening of the chapter, and set it against the wilderness: as Israel was miraculously supplied with water in the desert, so the God who has become their salvation will open many and manifold springs of it, to draw from at their heart’s delight. Ellicott allows the clause to be either part of the hymn or an address to those who join in it, and prefers the second; he then describes the later ritual of the Feast of Tabernacles, in which the priests carried water from the Pool of Siloam in a golden vase to the Temple and poured it beside the altar of burnt offering while the people chanted the great hymn of praise. If that ceremony represents the ritual of the monarchy, he says, the prophet’s words may point at it, and the Talmud expressly connects the act with this symbolism.

Calvin turns the clause into a metaphor of supply: the salvation of God is set before them like a constantly running fountain, and since nothing in life is more necessary than water, the part stands for the whole, so that all that supports life flows from God’s undeserved goodness. His mercy satisfies the thirsty and revives the worn out, and we ought to be like dry ground desiring the waters of the Lord; God does not leave us burning with unsatisfied desire but sets fountains before us, and that is Christ, of whose fulness all receive. Gill fills out the equation: the water is grace, so called because it softens, purifies, cools and extinguishes thirst; the well is deep and not within everyone’s reach, the bucket is faith and is itself God’s gift, and the drawing is done in the use of means, in prayer and reading and attendance on the word. Wesley says only that thirsty souls are filled with graces drawn from God in gospel ordinances.
4:
Matthew Henry calls this the second part of the song and marks the change of direction: in the first part believers stir up themselves, here they encourage one another and spread the praise further. He identifies the addressees as the inhabitants of Zion, whom God had particularly protected, and lays down the principle that those who have received distinguishing favours ought to be the most forward in praising. On the manner of praising he gives two heads. The first is prayer, since giving thanks for former mercy is a decent way of begging further mercy, which is itself accepted as a thankful acknowledgment. The second is preaching and writing, since we must not only speak to God but to others concerning him, and not only call upon his name but proclaim it.

John Calvin takes the same turn outward and presses it two ways, that they should speak not to one but to all, and not at one time only but throughout their whole life. He uses the phrase about calling on the name to define worship, since Scripture frequently puts that one act for the whole, showing where our confidence is placed. The deliverance he thinks too excellent to be proclaimed in a corner, so that it must go through the whole world, first to the Jews and then to all, which makes this exhortation a forerunner of gospel preaching. Adam Clarke reads the clause as a commission to preach him who is the Root of Jesse and stands as an ensign for the nations. Charles Ellicott asks where the words came from, rendering the phrase literally among the peoples and noting that the prophet quotes the hymn sung when the Ark was placed in Zion, and in part a psalm.

John Gill keeps the singing concrete, psalms and hymns sung vocally and together as churches do, though he allows a second construction by which the Lord himself is the subject matter of the song. Ellicott hears in the reason given for singing another echo of the older song, in which God is said to have triumphed gloriously. Calvin warns that those who exhort others must not sit down in indolence, nothing being more absurd than lazy men stirring up others to praise God; and insists there is abundant ground for the singing, since God holds out a rich subject of it, the work of reconciling us to himself and destroying the dominion of death; that the thing is known in all the earth he takes as a glance at the calling of the Gentiles.

The last verse gathers the chapter to a point. Clarke widens the address beyond the Jewish people to all members of the church, since the Holy One of Israel dwells in them, and supports it from the apostle’s summary of the mystery proclaimed among the Gentiles, Christ in you, the hope of glory. Ellicott notes again that the Hebrew is feminine, the inhabitant being the daughter of Zion, the restored church that has Zion for her dwelling-place, and observes that the hymn closes with the divine title characteristic of this prophet, whose presence was to be a joy to the remnant worthy of their calling; with it, he adds, what has been called the Immanuel volume of the prophecies comes to its close. Calvin makes the title do two things: the Holy One, so that reverence may not be mere terror but the mark of a peculiar care, and of Israel from the effect, since by gathering and saving a people God may be said to have become their own property. Our whole happiness, he says, is to have God dwelling with us, and without that a life full of riches would still be wretched; his presence fills us with inconceivable joy, his absence leaves us exposed to grief. Gill ends where the verse does, with the high praises of God sung aloud.
